title: Chapter 1.  Geography — The Meghalaya Plateau & the Wettest Place on Earth

blocks.content: Meghalaya's name literally means 'Abode of Clouds', and its geography chapter is dominated by a single, world-famous superlative: it is home to the wettest place(s) on Earth. This chapter also covers the Meghalaya Plateau's distinctive geology and its famous limestone cave systems.

Meghalaya lies in India's north-east, almost entirely surrounded by Assam to its north and east, and bordered by Bangladesh to its south and west - giving it an unusual geography as a state nearly enclosed by a single other Indian state on one side and an international border on the other.

The state is physiographically dominated by the Meghalaya Plateau (also called the Shillong Plateau), an ancient block of Precambrian crystalline rock - geologically related to, and considered a detached extension of, the peninsular Indian plateau (the same ancient landmass that includes the Chota Nagpur Plateau covered in the companion Jharkhand GS volume) - separated from the main peninsular block by the intervening Garo-Rajmahal Gap, now filled by the Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains.

The plateau itself is conventionally divided into three sub-regions, corresponding closely to the state's three principal tribal communities and traditional hill divisions: the Garo Hills (west), the Khasi Hills (centre), and the Jaintia Hills (east).

cells: Assam (north and east); Bangladesh (south and west, international border)
Meghalaya (Shillong) Plateau - geologically an extension of the peninsular Indian plateau
Shillong Peak, approx 1,965 m, near the state capital

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 'Meghalaya' means 'Abode of Clouds' in Sanskrit - a name that directly reflects the state's exceptional rainfall (below), a frequently tested etymology fact.

Mawsynram, a village in the Khasi Hills near Shillong, is officially recognised by the Guinness Book of World Records as receiving the highest average annual rainfall of any inhabited place on Earth, with figures typically cited in the range of 11,000-12,000 mm per year.

Nearby Cherrapunji (locally known as Sohra) held this 'wettest place on Earth' record for a long period and remains world-famous for its extreme rainfall, and additionally holds the separate world record for the highest rainfall recorded within a single calendar month and within a single calendar year (both set in 1861) - meaning Cherrapunji and Mawsynram hold DIFFERENT specific rainfall records, a frequently confused distinction.

This extreme, highly concentrated monsoon rainfall results from the direct funnelling effect of moist Bay of Bengal air being forced upward against the southern face of the Khasi Hills' steep escarpment, a textbook example of orographic (relief) rainfall in Indian geography.

cells: Highest AVERAGE ANNUAL rainfall of any inhabited place on Earth (Guinness World Record)
Located in the Khasi Hills, near Shillong
Highest rainfall in a single MONTH and a single CALENDAR YEAR (both records set in 1861)
Formerly held the 'wettest place' title before Mawsynram; still world-famous for extreme rainfall

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Mawsynram (highest AVERAGE annual rainfall) and Cherrapunji (highest rainfall in a single MONTH/YEAR, both records from 1861) hold DIFFERENT world rainfall records - this precise distinction is one of the most frequently tested and most frequently MIS-stated facts about Meghalaya.

items: Living root bridges - a unique, centuries-old Khasi and Jaintia engineering tradition in which the aerial roots of the rubber fig tree (Ficus elastica) are deliberately trained, over decades, across streams and rivers to form living, strengthening, self-repairing pedestrian bridges - are one of Meghalaya's most globally distinctive features, found particularly around villages in the southern Khasi Hills such as Nongriat (home to the famous 'Double-Decker' root bridge).

Meghalaya's limestone geology (particularly in the Jaintia Hills) has produced one of the most extensive cave systems in the Indian subcontinent, with several of India's longest documented cave systems located in the state, including Krem Liat Prah (widely cited as India's longest cave system) - making Meghalaya a major centre for Indian speleology (cave science/exploration).

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Krem Liat Prah, in the Jaintia Hills, is widely cited as INDIA's longest cave system - a frequently tested superlative linking Meghalaya's limestone geology to national-level cave-system rankings.

items: Meghalaya: approx 22,429 sq km; borders Assam and Bangladesh; capital: Shillong. 'Meghalaya' means 'Abode of Clouds'.
Three traditional hill divisions: Garo Hills (west), Khasi Hills (centre), Jaintia Hills (east); highest point: Shillong Peak (~1,965 m).
Mawsynram = highest AVERAGE ANNUAL rainfall of any inhabited place on Earth; Cherrapunji (Sohra) = highest rainfall in a single month/year (1861 records) - DIFFERENT records.
Living root bridges (Ficus elastica) - a unique Khasi/Jaintia engineering tradition, e.g. the 'Double-Decker' root bridge at Nongriat.
Krem Liat Prah (Jaintia Hills) = widely cited as India's longest cave system, part of Meghalaya's extensive limestone cave network.
